message.content:
In Texas, tenants have several statutory protections and responsibilities under the Texas Property Code and related laws. Below is an overview of key rights you typically enjoy as a renter: | Category | Typical Tenant Rights (Texas) | Notes | |----------|------------------------------|-------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | Landlords must provide a written receipt and itemized list of deductions if any. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a safe, sanitary condition, including functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, and structural integrity.
• Must comply with local health and building codes. | If the landlord fails to repair, you may withhold rent or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct remedy. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord does not fix a major issue within a reasonable time after notice, you may pay for repairs and deduct the cost from your rent. | Must give written notice and keep receipts; deduction cannot exceed the amount of the repair. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | Landlords cannot enter without proper notice (usually 24–48 hours). | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑renewal or termination of a month‑to‑month lease, landlords must give at least 30 days’ written notice.
• For eviction due to nonpayment, the landlord must serve a 3‑day notice (or 5 days for certain cases). | Notice must be in writing and delivered personally or via certified mail. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the court process: serve notice → file complaint → court hearing → judgment. | Evictions for nonpayment require a 3‑day notice; for other reasons, a 30‑day notice may be required. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much a landlord can raise rent, but must provide proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month). | Some cities have local rent‑control ordinances that may apply. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | Covered under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Civil Rights Act. | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease agreements must be in writing for leases longer than one year. | Oral agreements are enforceable but harder to prove. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide hot water, electricity, and gas unless otherwise specified. | Tenants may be responsible for other utilities per lease terms. | | **Maintenance Responsibilities** | • Tenants must keep the unit clean, dispose of trash properly, and avoid damage. | Failure to do so can lead to deductions from the security deposit. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Ensure it complies with Texas law and includes all required disclosures (e.g., lead paint notice if applicable). 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of notices, receipts, and photos of any maintenance issues. 3. **Give Written Notice** – When reporting problems or terminating tenancy, use written communication and keep copies. 4. **Know Local Ordinances** – Some Texas cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas, Houston) have additional tenant protections such as rent‑control or mandatory disclosure requirements. 5. **Seek Legal Advice** – If you face eviction or disputes, consult a tenant‑rights organization or attorney. --- If you need a specific lease template or a legal document tailored to your situation, let me know the details (type of contract, parties, and any special provisions), and I can generate a draft for you.
